### 4.171 Token default DACL state and process ownership (2026-10-01)

`SetTokenInformation(TokenDefaultDacl)` now captures a private ACL snapshot,
validates its bounds and standard allow/deny/audit/alarm SIDs, and replaces
the token's policy. NULL and empty ACLs remain distinct. Querying the class
returns an ABI-correct pointer into the caller's buffer, including the full
ACL capacity; no kernel or original guest pointer escapes. Short input,
inaccessible storage, invalid ACLs and missing TOKEN_ADJUST_DEFAULT rights
fail without changing the previous policy.

ACL snapshots are immutable and reference counted. Publication and pinning
use a short IRQ-safe lock; allocation, reclamation and guest-memory access
occur outside it. DuplicateHandle shares token state. DuplicateTokenEx and
CreateRestrictedToken retain the snapshot but subsequent policy replacements
are independent. TokenStatistics now has unique TokenId/ModifiedId values;
DACL updates change ModifiedId, and dynamic storage accounting reflects the
default ACL and primary-group identifier rather than always reporting zero.

Primary tokens are owned by NT process objects instead of OpenProcessToken
returning one global identity. Ordinary child creation snapshots the parent
token before starting the child. Opening a retained exited-process handle
can still obtain its token; closing the last process/thread reference reclaims
that ownership, while a separately opened token handle remains valid. Root
shell launches reset their identity at their execution boundary. Process-token
lookups pin under the existing BSP serialization, including handle validation,
so another Win32 thread cannot recycle the process slot between those steps.
Reference scans skip never-allocated thread slots.

The new `token_policy_pe.c` fixture runs unchanged on Windows and OsitoK.
It covers setter capture, getter buffer negotiation, duplicate-handle sharing,
token/filter isolation, malformed ACL/SID rejection, access rights, ModifiedId,
process-token reopening, suspended-child inheritance, parent/child mutation
isolation, exited-process lifetime and concurrent query/set/duplication.
Both workers synchronize their start and yield during 2,048 operations each.
A 65,532-byte ACL is accepted and round-tripped on OsitoK; the Windows reference
instead reports ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED, preserving its previous policy.
That platform resource quota is not reproduced as an artificial fixed cap.

- `token-policy-concurrent-20261001`: both architectures pass the final fixture;
  GDB reports TOKEN-LIVE=0 and POLICY-LIVE=0 after each executable, and SSH works.
- `token-policy-positive-20261001-verified`,
  `token-policy-access-regression-20261001`,
  `token-policy-cycles-regression-20261001`, and
  `token-policy-restricted-regression-20261001`: policy, AccessCheck,
  process/thread cycle accounting and restricted-token regressions pass on

### 4.172 Job object lifetime, inheritance and commitment (2026-10-01)

The previous Steam trace failed Job setup because class 4 was rejected even
for an empty UI restriction mask. Job APIs now live in `ntjob.c`, with dynamic
objects and PID-based membership instead of fixed eight-entry arrays. Basic
and extended limit layouts use their actual PE32/PE64 sizes: 48/64 and 112/144
bytes respectively. UI mask zero succeeds; unsupported nonzero restrictions
still fail explicitly. Class 2 updates preserve existing extended limits.

Job references distinguish numeric handle entries, inherited handle owners
and process membership. Common handle-table cleanup releases Job ownership,
including NtClose, duplicated handles and forced process teardown. Last-handle
close enforces KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE without recursively terminating an already
terminating Job. A Job without that flag remains alive while members exist.
Queries and termination use process IDs rather than handles in the creator's
namespace. Short IRQ-disabled metadata transactions do not span guest memory
access, allocation or member termination.

Active-process quotas, ordinary child inheritance, permitted breakaway and
silent breakaway are enforced before a child runs. Inherit-all creation now
copies all marked handle owners transactionally, rather than silently keeping
only a small explicit snapshot. Extended process/Job memory limits charge
private VM backing through the shared VM tracking path. Decommit, release and
process exit return that commitment; repeated commitment is not charged twice.
Heap growth and thread stacks use that path, and per-process/Job peaks remain
available after a member exits. This does not yet account direct PE image
backing or section/COW commitment.

The new lifetime fixture exposed a separate teardown race: child completion
was signaled before PE, VM and environment cleanup finished. A waiting parent
could close/reuse the NT process slot while the old child context still
referenced it. Completion and removal of the child context are now published
together after cleanup, including forced termination. Forced exit also drops
the child's inherited handle owners.

`job_object_pe.c` runs unchanged on native Windows and OsitoK. It covers 20
simultaneous Jobs, layouts, access rights, UI mask validation, active limits,
duplicate/NtClose lifetime, inherited child handles, permitted/denied
breakaway, last inherited handle close, explicit termination, memory peaks,
reserve/commit/decommit/recommit behavior and heap quota failure. Two live
processes exercise an aggregate Job quota, then prove exit returns capacity.
The Windows runner itself belongs to an ambient Job, so membership assertions
query the specific test Job. Native active-limit rejection of a suspended
process differs from OsitoK's termination behavior; that result is logged,
not claimed as identical exit-status behavior.

### 4.173 Selected process primary tokens (2026-10-01)

CreateProcessAsUserW no longer rejects every filtered token or silently calls
CreateProcessW under the parent's identity. It pins the supplied token with
TOKEN_QUERY, TOKEN_DUPLICATE and TOKEN_ASSIGN_PRIMARY rights, then carries
that explicit source through KERNEL32, the child launcher and NT process
allocation. The child owns an independent primary-token copy before it can
run, including deny-only groups, restricting SIDs and default-DACL policy.
There is no global temporary identity or parent-token replacement. NULL token
still selects ordinary primary-token inheritance, not thread impersonation.

The local model has no SE_ASSIGNPRIMARYTOKEN privilege. Assignment checks
same-logon/user identity, preserves existing deny constraints and refuses to
restore grants or weaken an existing restricting-SID set. A restricted child
given an inheritable handle to the parent's unrestricted token receives
ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD when trying to create a less-restricted process.
Foreign identities remain unsupported. A valid impersonation-level token
can be copied into a primary token, matching the measured Windows behavior;
identification-level input fails with ERROR_BAD_IMPERSONATION_LEVEL.

The API validates output/startup storage and SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES layout.
Custom process/thread security descriptors fail explicitly instead of being
ignored. Inheritance flags on the returned process/thread handles are set
before publishing PROCESS_INFORMATION to guest memory. Process object ACL
assignment and general object authorization are not implemented by this
change; owning a restricted token is not a completed security boundary.

`process_token_pe.c` is the same source on Windows and OsitoK. It checks the
selected token while suspended and from inside the child after RevertToSelf,
two-pass AccessCheck behavior, deny-only attributes, token type, independent
default-DACL snapshots, source-handle closure and exited-token lifetime.
An ordinary suspended grandchild inherits the restricted primary token.
The fixture also checks NULL-token creation, source-token handle rights,
invalid handles, accepted/rejected impersonation levels, returned handle
inheritance and attempted restoration of the parent's unrestricted identity.
Twelve additional selected-token launches exercise teardown and reuse.

The native loader needs an initial thread identity with sufficient access,
as in Chromium's broker flow. The fixture supplies a more permissive but
still restricted impersonation token, verifies its level, and reverts at
entry before checking the process identity. Early native iterations record
STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED and STATUS_BAD_IMPERSONATION_LEVEL before entry when
this setup was absent or the initial token lacked restricting SIDs. Those
failed references were retained; they are not counted as successful tests.

### 4.174 Published NTDLL exports and PE32 output widths (2026-10-01)

The synthetic NTDLL facade now contains a real PE export directory, address
table, sorted case-sensitive name table and name-ordinal table. These are
generated from the existing co-located export descriptors, not from a Steam
function list. Each EAT target is an executable entry within the process-local
image: PE64 preserves the existing patch window and import-boundary IF rule;
PE32 jumps to its typed compat gateway without altering the caller's stack.
Nt/Zw aliases share a target. GetProcAddress, LdrGetProcedureAddress and static
imports use the published entries, including the ordinals discovered in the
image. Headers/metadata are read-only, metadata is NX and code is RX. Facade
construction fails before publication on invalid descriptors, exhausted image
space, thunk failure or protection failure. Unload follows existing ownership.

Publication is explicitly enabled for NTDLL only. Its generated ordinals are
descriptor index + 1, not the ordinal inventory of a particular Windows build.
Other providers retain their existing ordinal resolvers and dynamic-data
behavior. The builder rejects data descriptors; this does not claim that CRT
storage, ordinal-only exports, forwarders or all shim DLL images are complete.
The existing 64 KiB facade and 1,024-thunk capacity remain bounded; enabling a
larger provider requires a layout/capacity change rather than truncation.

All ABI registry providers are now evaluated before their count is passed to
registration. The old expression read `n` in another argument to the same call
that invoked a provider writing `n`, relying on argument evaluation order.

The native-reference fixture exposed two additional PE32 ABI defects:
NtQueryInformationProcess used the 48-byte native basic-information layout,
and LdrGetProcedureAddress treated ANSI_STRING/output pointers as 64-bit.
The former now translates into the 24-byte PE32 layout and reports the target's
actual low PEB address when available, without truncating the native inspection
PEB. The latter reads counted ANSI_STRING32 names and writes exactly four
output bytes, with readable/writable range validation. The native paths and
explicit NtWow64QueryInformationProcess64 remain separate.

`shim_exports_pe.c` is compiled unchanged for Windows and OsitoK. It validates
bounded/sorted tables, all named and ordinal addresses, IAT/EAT identity,
missing names, case sensitivity, direct NT calls, counted loader strings,
output canaries, protections and repeated LoadLibrary references. Four child
processes per bitness repeat the contract, modify a private export-metadata
page and exit; the parent's image must remain unchanged. Windows PE32 places
its export directory on an executable read-only page, so the portable test
permits read-only or execute-read metadata, not writable metadata.

### 4.175 Suspended child image preparation (2026-10-01)

CreateProcess now waits for kernel-side child preparation before returning its
handles. Even with CREATE_SUSPENDED, the child's private address space contains
the relocated EXE, its actual PEB image base, initial stack and final image
protections. The initial guest thread remains behind a gate: imported DLL entry
points, TLS callbacks and the EXE entry point do not execute until ResumeThread.
Preparation failure is returned synchronously instead of publishing a process
whose image is absent. STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT now translates to
ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT rather than the default unknown-status error 317.

The PE loader separates mapping/publication from import binding. Ordinary root
and DLL loads still use the combined wrapper and existing abort cleanup. A
prepared child's later IAT/CFG writes validate PE ownership and the mapped PTE,
temporarily unprotect only the containing page when necessary, then restore its
permissions before further import resolution. Both native and compat32 IAT
writes use this path; final protections are not reapplied over the broker's
patches after resume. This is not a blanket RWX image workaround.

The creation handshake pins the child context until the creator copies its
result. A disappeared creator cannot hold that acknowledgement indefinitely.
The suspended gate uses scheduler sleeps and honors cooperative termination;
early failures and termination before resume follow process-owned cleanup.
NT completion is published after teardown and before the child slot is reused.

`suspended_image_pe.c` is compiled unchanged for native Windows and OsitoK, with
a companion DLL and a real TLS callback. Per architecture, eight children check
the remote PEB/MZ header, read-only headers, RX code, initial data, absence of
entry/TLS/DllMain execution while suspended, private parent/child images, remote
data/constant patches, four resumes and four pre-resume terminations. Resumed
children verify that the patches survived import binding, TLS ran once after
the patch, and the dependency attached. Four malformed-image launches exercise
synchronous failure and slot reuse. Windows classifies this MZ-only fixture as
unsupported DOS (216); OsitoK rejects the malformed PE (193). The fixture also
checks the exact NTSTATUS-to-193 translation on both systems.

### 4.176 Process-owned remote virtual memory (2026-10-01)

VirtualAllocEx, VirtualFreeEx, VirtualProtectEx and VirtualQueryEx no longer
validate the target handle and then operate on the caller. Their NT handlers
resolve the selected process, enforce VM_OPERATION or QUERY_INFORMATION, and
carry its Win32 owner ID, CR3 and compatible address limits through the VM
operation. Kernel32 calls the native-width handlers directly; NTDLL retains
PE32 in/out thunking, including the 28-byte MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION layout.
Neither implementation switches the caller's identity or address space.

Reservation, commit, decommit, release, private protections, PE protections,
query, collision detection and Job commit accounting now use the target owner.
Collision checks include target PE mappings, private VMAs, unfaulted Linux mmap
reservations and mapped pages; root PE32 identity exclusions remain intact.
Explicit MEM_RESERVE rounds the base down to the 64 KiB allocation boundary;
commit and range sizes retain page alignment. NULL-base MEM_COMMIT implicitly
reserves in the target. Released/decommitted backing remains target-owned.

The existing BSP-owned Win32 execution model serializes handle resolution and
the non-yielding VM operation in one IRQ-disabled interval. Teardown marks the
process closed to new remote VM operations before unmapping resources. An
exited process handle remains queryable for its exit status, but cannot regain
an address space through allocation. Current-process pseudo handles remain
available to internal cleanup. This is not a new general SMP process reference
mechanism; that assumption must be revisited before running Win32 on APs.

`remote_vm_pe.c` runs unchanged on native Windows and OsitoK. Each architecture
creates four pairs of suspended children while the parent holds the same fixed
VA with a sentinel value. It tests reserve-only state, unaligned reserve,
commit subsets, zero fill, decommit/recommit, invalid release size, private
contents/protections, independent siblings, NT pointer-width canaries,
restricted process-handle rights, NULL-base commit, invalid and exited handles,
resumed child access/free, termination with live backing, and parent survival.
Image-header PAGE_NOACCESS/restoration additionally proves that remote image
protection does not modify the parent's image. Four resumed children pass.

The 4.175 fixture's original QueryEx/ProtectEx checks were insufficient to
establish isolation: parent and child images used the same VA and original
permissions. Its pre-resume image, remote reads/writes, TLS and loader evidence
stands, but the stronger remote protection claim is established only here.

### 4.177. NtOpenThread, shared thread identity and suspended-child NTDLL

The 4.176 natural-launch trace stopped while resolving `NtOpenThread`. NTDLL
now publishes callable `NtOpenThread` / `ZwOpenThread` exports with four-argument
stdcall metadata. The wrapper probes caller buffers and marshals 32-bit
CLIENT_ID, OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES and handle outputs separately from the native
64-bit ABI. Invalid IDs, mismatched process IDs, named opens, invalid pointers
and access masks return statuses validated against native Windows. RootDirectory
does not affect CID lookup. OBJ_INHERIT is recorded on the caller-owned handle.

The implementation also repairs an underlying identity mismatch: NT worker
objects previously used per-process counters, while CreateThread returned a
different global counter, and every child primary initially had TID 1. Child
primaries and workers now allocate from one NT namespace, with the same ID in
the object, execution context, TEB and API results. The legacy shell-launched
primary still uses TID 1. The allocator fails on ID-space exhaustion instead
of wrapping onto a live ID. Lookup and handle publication run without BSP
preemption, consistently with current Win32 ownership; this is not an AP-safe
general object reference mechanism.

`OpenThread` delegates to the same object lookup rather than substituting the
root primary object for a child's main thread. Generic access is mapped to
thread rights, including implied limited-query/set and resume rights. Querying
identity/exit status and resuming enforce their handle rights. CreateThread no
longer reports a pseudo-handle success when NT object allocation fails; scheduler
setup failures release the allocated object/handle and mappings. A terminated
thread remains queryable through retained or duplicated handles and can be
reopened while those handles exist. A terminated unreferenced slot cannot be
reopened merely because its owning process object is still retained.

`open_thread_pe.c` runs unchanged on native Windows and OsitoK, x86 and x64.
It covers both exports, pointer-width canaries, full/TID-only client IDs,
generic and invalid access masks, input/output faults, inheritance, four worker
lifecycles, closing the creation handle before resume, duplicated exit-state
retention, denied query/resume, globally distinct suspended child primary IDs,
sibling mismatch and primary-thread handle lifetime after process termination.
Retirement polls are bounded: Windows can signal a process before dropping its
last internal thread reference, so process signaling alone is not a thread
destruction barrier.

### 4.178. NTDLL bootstrap before the initial-thread suspension gate

`dll_prepare_process` now maps and pins the registered NTDLL image after the
main EXE is published and before import binding. Both the root winexec path
and CreateProcess use this step; the child completes it before reporting
creation_ready, without running dependency DllMain, application TLS callbacks
or the EXE entry. The preparation rejects a missing export provider or a
provider with a lifecycle callback, so this phase cannot accidentally execute
guest initialization. Resume binds imports against the existing image rather
than replacing the parent's pre-resume modifications.

The core image uses a common ABI-wide virtual address (0x7FFB0000 for PE32,
0x6FFFFFFF0000 for PE32+) with separate physical pages and protections for each
owner. These are loader policy addresses, not Steam-specific addresses. The
general PE allocator can relocate on conflict; core mapping detects that
result, releases the alternate allocation and fails with
STATUS_CONFLICTING_ADDRESSES instead of silently publishing a different base
or overwriting the executable. Pinning prevents FreeLibrary from removing the
core image, while normal process teardown still releases it. This is not
system-image ASLR, full KnownDlls section sharing, or a complete native Windows
loader implementation.

The existing suspended-image fixture now verifies NTDLL's header, the common
address of NtOpenThread, all 32 bytes of its entry, RX/MEM_IMAGE classification,
a private header-page patch and restored protection. The patch must survive
ResumeThread and an NT query must remain callable. Existing assertions still
require dependency/TLS/EXE code not to have run before resume, then to run once
after it. Eight child cycles include four pre-resume terminations. A copied
fixed-base fixture also requests the parent's NTDLL address: three failed
creations must be followed by successful ordinary creations. Native Windows
x64 returns error 487; WOW64 reports 308 for this PE32 case. OsitoK's non-WOW64
loader returns 487 in both ABIs. The fixture permits that documented difference.

### 4.179. Relocatable native x64 NT system-service entries

PE64 NTDLL Nt/Zw exports now use real `mov r10,rcx; mov eax,id; syscall; ret`
entries instead of the generic NOP/jump import facade. Both the EAT and import
resolver expose the same entry; aliases for the same implementation share the
service ID. A copied 32-byte entry remains callable at a different address.
IDs belong to an OsitoK build-private namespace, not to Windows' versioned
service-number tables. PE32 entries and non-service exports keep their prior
ABI. No Steam binary or application-specific entry point is patched by the OS.

LSTAR routes only that namespace to `nt64_service_entry`. The existing ELF
dispatch path and its stack/frame cursors are unchanged. The NT gateway keeps
its frame on the calling thread's stack, saves nonvolatile GPRs and FXSAVE
state, clears DF, enables interrupts for waits/callbacks, and invokes the
registered Microsoft-x64 handler through a bounded integer/pointer argument
adapter. Extra stack arguments are probed before copying. Invalid service IDs
or a caller without a readable PE64 image are rejected. The dispatcher chooses
the implementation from kernel-owned descriptors, never a guest target pointer.
Current NT exports' metadata gives their scalar/pointer argument count; adding
an API whose PE32 DWORD count differs from its x64 arity needs explicit metadata
rather than assuming those counts are interchangeable.

This preserves the current CPL0 PE execution model and its interrupt-enabled
import boundary. It is not a CPL3 syscall transition, protected kernel stack,
complete NT exception/unwind implementation, or security boundary. All frame
state is stack-local; no new global cursor must be unwound after termination.
Concurrent waits and process exit are tested, but arbitrary nested user
callbacks/non-local unwinds are not comprehensively qualified here.

The same no-CRT `nt64-service.exe` runs on Windows and OsitoK. It checks copied
services with 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 11 arguments; file create/write/read/close;
virtual allocation/free; output-size validation; nonvolatile GPR/XMM canaries;
an inaccessible fifth stack argument; an unknown service ID; four concurrent
query/delay callers; and protected NTDLL interception in a suspended child.
The child calls the interceptor and its relocated original while the parent's
entry remains unchanged. The fixture measures the interceptor-call delta,
since Windows itself can invoke it before the child's main entry.

The native ELF companion checks six-argument mmap, IDs, yields, memory protect,
unmap, unknown-number ENOSYS and output before/after the PE test. Like existing
OsitoK freestanding ELF fixtures it uses `-mno-red-zone`; this is not a claim
that arbitrary Linux binaries have a protected red zone in the CPL0 model.

### 4.180. Native process opens, identity access and inherited handles

NTDLL now exports NtOpenProcess and ZwOpenProcess over the existing process
objects. PE64 uses the relocatable native service entries from 4.179; PE32 uses
the compatibility ABI. Process/thread opens share the same probed CLIENT_ID and
OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES marshaller. Native failures preserve the output handle;
WOW64 keeps its early validation/initialization ordering and four-byte output.
Null/named objects, inaccessible inputs, native misalignment and nonrepresentable
PIDs/TIDs are rejected without dereferencing an unchecked guest pointer.

Process lookup requires a nonzero PID. An optional TID must belong to that
process, unlike NtOpenThread's TID-only lookup. Lookup and handle publication
run under the existing process-table interrupt guard. Referenced exited objects
remain openable; unreferenced retired identities do not resolve to reused table
slots. Internal pseudo-handle duplication retains its already-granted-access
path rather than accidentally inheriting user-open validation rules.

OpenProcess now honors inheritance and shares generic/implied access mapping
with the NT entry. Query/set information imply their limited counterparts.
GetProcessId, GetExitCodeProcess and NtQueryInformationProcess enforce query
rights; internal identity resolution remains independent of those public query
permissions. Native/WOW64 memory reads require VM_READ and native writes require
VM_WRITE, through the existing live-process resolver. A query-only handle no
longer grants access to a child's memory. This does not establish complete
Win32 WriteProcessMemory protection semantics, process-object DACL evaluation,
SeDebugPrivilege authorization, protected processes or a security boundary.
The existing CPL0 compatibility model and restricted-token limitations remain.

`open_process_pe.c` is the same no-CRT fixture on Windows and OsitoK. It covers
PID/full CID/mismatched TID lookup; Nt/Zw aliases; generic and implied grants;
invalid access masks; output-width guards; object-attribute and pointer errors;
NT/Win32 inheritance; restricted identity/memory access; and four child cycles.
Two children resume and verify their inherited parent handle, and two terminate
while suspended. Opened/duplicated process handles survive closing the original
CreateProcess handle, retain wait/exit identity and retire the CID on final close.

### 4.181 Native process/thread token opens (2026-10-01)

The four NtOpenProcessToken[Ex]/NtOpenThreadToken[Ex] entries and their Zw aliases
now use the same token objects as ADVAPI32. The SysV core returns NTSTATUS without
changing LastError. Both guest ABIs probe output memory, preserve native failure
output (WOW64 clears its four-byte output), and never truncate a native pseudo
handle. Thread lookup checks query/limited-query rights and pins the selected
impersonation token before the source handle or thread slot can be recycled.
Process token handles continue to reference the selected child after it exits.

OpenAsSelf avoids the caller's low-level impersonation context; anonymous targets
cannot be opened. The Win32 wrappers now share these level and source-access
checks. Generic token grants match the native reference, invalid rights fail,
ACCESS_SYSTEM_SECURITY requires a privilege the local identity does not have,
and OBJ_INHERIT is applied to the new handle. The current local token model still
does not evaluate a separate token-object security descriptor on open. Token
default DACLs describe newly created objects and are not substituted for that
missing policy. This is not complete multi-user authorization or a sandbox
security boundary; the CPL0 and object-DACL limitations in 4.180 remain.

### 4.182 Native thread impersonation-token assignment (2026-10-01)

NtSetInformationThread and ZwSetInformationThread now implement
ThreadImpersonationToken (class 5), using the same assignment core as Win32
SetThreadToken. The thread handle needs THREAD_SET_THREAD_TOKEN (0x80), and the
token handle needs TOKEN_IMPERSONATE. Primary tokens are rejected with
STATUS_BAD_TOKEN_TYPE; null tokens remove impersonation. The selected thread and
token are resolved while the existing BSP interrupt guard protects their handle
and object lifetimes. Assignment transfers a pinned reference to the thread and
releases the prior reference afterward. An exited thread retained by an open
handle remains assignable, as measured on Windows; final destruction releases
its assigned token. No application-specific branch or sandbox bypass was added.

NT calls preserve LastError; the Win32 wrapper translates failure status. Native
input is exactly one eight-byte handle with DWORD alignment. WOW64 accepts at
least four bytes and reads only its four-byte handle, including unaligned input.
Guest ranges are checked before reading, and native handles are not truncated.
All other information classes still return STATUS_INVALID_INFO_CLASS. This is
not a complete priority, affinity, debugging or thread-information implementation,
nor does it remove the object-DACL and CPL0 limitations documented above.

The same thread_info_pe.c binaries assert these results on Windows and OsitoK:
current and selected-child identity, Nt/Zw revert, source and token access
rights, wrong object types, NT/Win32 errors, pointer/length/alignment rules and
three suspended-child exit cycles. The cycles retain a token independently of
the original handle, reassign an exited thread, and close every reference.

### 4.183 Job completion-port association and notifications (2026-10-01)

The 4.182 natural Steam failure was a real rejected operation:
SetInformationJobObject(JobObjectAssociateCompletionPortInformation, class 7).
The new implementation retains the selected IOCP object through an internal,
non-inheritable subsystem handle. It does not retain only the caller's numeric
handle: closing the original, duplicating it, or reusing that handle number must
not redirect or destroy the job's notification destination. IOCP lookup now
follows the backing event's identity. Final event destruction, including NtClose
and forced process cleanup, releases the port slot and active-thread allocation.
Creator teardown no longer destroys a port still referenced by another owner.

The association checks JOB_OBJECT_SET_ATTRIBUTES and IO_COMPLETION_MODIFY_STATE.
Invalid handles, ordinary events, restricted rights, invalid guest buffers and
wrong lengths fail explicitly. Native input must be exactly 16 bytes; WOW64
accepts at least 8 and reads only those bytes. Native completion keys keep all
64 bits. A second active association fails; a null port detaches and releases
the reference. Class 7 is set-only. Successful association preserves LastError,
as measured with the same PE fixtures on Windows.

Jobs post NEW_PROCESS, EXIT_PROCESS or ABNORMAL_EXIT_PROCESS, and
ACTIVE_PROCESS_ZERO with the associated key and process ID. Late association
reports existing members. Active-process and private-commit limit failures post
their corresponding messages. The abnormal-exit classification uses the listed
NT exception statuses, not every nonzero or negative exit code. Internal posting
never accesses the exiting process's TEB: notification can run after its address
space has been released. The public Win32 enqueue wrapper alone translates an
enqueue error to LastError. Ordinary job notification delivery remains best
effort; it does not make the bounded port queue lossless.

### 4.184 Token integrity-label state and the next natural-launch failure

Chromium's exit code 7006 is SBOX_FATAL_INTEGRITY. The saved hardware log from
4.183 also contains eight rejections of SetTokenInformation class 25 on
restricted tokens. These are distinct from the later global handle exhaustion.

TokenIntegrityLevel now belongs to the token object. Native and WOW64 setters
capture and validate the caller's label/SID, require TOKEN_ADJUST_DEFAULT, allow
lowering, and reject an elevation with ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD. The local
identity has no SeTcbPrivilege. DuplicateHandle aliases see the same state;
DuplicateTokenEx/CreateRestrictedToken snapshot it. Assignment to a suspended
child and retaining its token after process exit preserve that object's state.
Queries return an owned, normalized S-1-16-RID label with attributes 0x60;
TokenGroups and TokenStatistics agree. ModifiedId changes, not TokenId.

The native fixture measures validation order, short/oversized ABI buffers,
inaccessible pointers, SID authority/revision/count, attribute normalization,
arbitrary RIDs, rights, and successful LastError preservation. This does not
implement general mandatory-integrity authorization, registry/object SACLs,
token object ACLs or all process-assignment integrity ceilings. Existing
AccessCheck rejects unsupported SACL policy; these passes are not a claim of
complete Chromium sandbox isolation or of ring-3 execution.

### 4.185 Uncached predefined-registry handles and remaining exhaustion

The next missing import is RegDisablePredefinedCache. steamwebhelper's call at
0x14003c7da uses IAT 0x14049a020; its return address matches the 4.184 null-fetch
faults. The executable extracted from the baseline image matches the previously
disassembled copy, SHA-256
f9ee1d1cc0f06fad16c9a277136a2e1b00b6b668901e28454a7dd8af29afde0d.

ADVAPI32 now exports RegDisablePredefinedCache and RegDisablePredefinedCacheEx
with zero-argument native/WOW64 contracts. The registry has no cache of opened
predefined-root handles: build_path/reg_key_context resolve each pseudo-handle
on every operation. Consequently both functions succeed without allocating
state, closing user handles, changing LastError or initializing/flushing the
persistent hive. A fictitious process flag would add no behavior here.

This is the cache-disable contract, not a claim that the existing flat registry
implements security-aware HKEY_CURRENT_USER/HKEY_USERS SID aliases. Per-user
hives, anonymous/impersonated registry authorization and true key-object handle
lifetimes remain separate limitations. No registry ACL or sandbox check is
bypassed by this change.

### 4.187 Mandatory-label ACE construction and the next sandbox stage

The null call identified in 4.186 is ADVAPI32 AddMandatoryAce. The new export
has the five-argument stdcall contract for PE32 and the native Win64 ABI.
It captures the label SID and a bounded ACL snapshot, validates before writing,
and appends a SYSTEM_MANDATORY_LABEL_ACE without replacing prior entries or
touching unused bytes. Successful LastError is preserved. SID authority,
revision, policy/flag masks, existing ACE bounds and available space are checked;
failures leave the caller's ACL unchanged. The shared ACL walker now accepts
revision 3 as well as 2 and 4, so queries can consume the resulting ACL.

Windows probes accept policy zero, SID subauthority counts 0 through 15,
requested revisions 0 through 4 (without lowering the ACL revision), and odd
ACL capacities when the new ACE fits. Invalid SID structure returns 1337,
non-label authority or invalid flag/policy bits return 87, excessive revision
returns 1306, malformed ACL returns 1336, and insufficient capacity returns 1344.
The native PE32/PE64 probe outputs agree. The constructor checks basic, label,
callback, object, compound and access-filter layouts; unrecognized ACE types
remain opaque and are preserved, not evaluated. Resource-attribute ACEs require
a relative-claim parser and explicitly return ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED without
mutation. That remaining limitation is not tested as Windows equivalence.

This change constructs caller-owned data only. It does not implement complete
mandatory integrity enforcement, resource-claim evaluation or sandbox isolation.
In particular, the existing GetSecurityInfo/SetSecurityInfo limitations are not
resolved, and AccessCheck still rejects unsupported security policy rather
than granting access. No application exception or sandbox failure is suppressed.

returns a handle; SetInformationJobObject(class 9, size 144) at helper return

call succeeds for 0x2108. The difference is
JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_DIE_ON_UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION (0x400). The captured bytes also
contain active-process limit 1 and a nonzero process-memory limit.

ntjob now includes that flag in the supported extended-limit mask. It is
stored and queried as job state, preserved by basic-limit updates, and
cleared by replacement extended limits. The existing PE32/PE64 exception
backend already runs VEH/SEH, permits handled continuations, and terminates
only the faulting process with the unhandled exception status. It has no WER
or error-dialog service to suppress. No handler is skipped and no exception
is swallowed by this change. Windows probes in job-error-reference-20261001-r1
show that setting/clearing this job flag does not change the visible
GetErrorMode bits; the unrelated SetErrorMode stub remains an open contract.

### 4.189 Job-private global atoms and namespace lifetime

The first implemented part of the pending UI contract is
JOB_OBJECT_UILIMIT_GLOBALATOMS (0x20). SetInformationJobObject class 4 now
stores this restriction, and QueryInformationJobObject returns it, including
queries of the current job through a null handle. Both successful class-4
operations preserve LastError. Invalid masks, invalid buffers and unsupported
restrictions leave the previous state intact. Other UI flags are still rejected
with ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED: neither 0x21 nor Chromium's full 0xff is accepted.

Each job gets a non-recycled 64-bit atom namespace ID on first use. Kernel32
global add/find/delete/name operations select that namespace when the bit is
enabled, or the original global namespace when it is disabled. Local atoms
remain per-process. String references, A/W calls, case-insensitive lookup and
integer atoms retain their existing behavior. Children that inherit membership
share the job table. The private table survives a temporary UI-bit clear and
also the exit of every member while a job handle remains open. Conversely,
closing the last job handle does not free atoms while member processes remain.
The final job release frees its private entries even if the bit was cleared.

Atom transactions now save/disable interrupts before taking the table lock,
and restore the prior IF afterward. Namespace selection happens under that
lock, preventing a BSP task switch between selecting and using job state.
Process and job cleanup use the same locking discipline. No USER window lookup,
compositor, clipboard, display mode, exception dispatcher or Steam launch flags
were changed in this increment.

The new job_ui_atoms_pe.c fixture and build-job-ui-atoms-test.sh run unchanged
on Windows and OsitoK in both ABIs. They test independent jobs, inherited
membership, local/global separation, A/W lookup/name/reference operations,
UI-bit toggles, handle/member retention, validation/access failures, and ten
destroyed jobs each leaving 64 private atoms. That exceeds the shared table's
512 slots over time and detects missing reclamation. An optional u:00000001
argument checks the still-unsupported masks without expecting Windows to reject
its own supported restrictions.

### 4.190 Job clipboard-data and display-setting restrictions

Class 4 now accepts READCLIPBOARD (0x02), WRITECLIPBOARD (0x04) and
DISPLAYSETTINGS (0x10), alongside the existing GLOBALATOMS (0x20). The
implemented mask is 0x36. Unsupported bits in 0xc9 still return
ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED, including Chromium's full 0xff request; invalid bits
outside 0xff return ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER. Neither failure changes the
previous restrictions. This is an enforced subset, not successful sandbox
initialization for Steam.

The new nt_job_ui_restrictions lookup uses the existing IRQ-saving job lock.
GetClipboardData and SetClipboardData check membership under the clipboard
transaction lock and deny restricted data access with error 5, including
delayed/null writes. Denied writes leave the clipboard sequence and data
unchanged. Registered-format metadata, availability and enumeration remain
accessible. Missing data on an unrestricted read sets ERROR_NOT_FOUND (1168).
ChangeDisplaySettings A/W reject restricted requests with DISP_CHANGE_FAILED
and error 5 before parsing/applying the requested mode, including CDS_TEST
and registry restoration. The Ex wrappers delegate to these paths; mode
enumeration and internal compositor/teardown restoration remain unchanged.

Native measurement exposed an important distinction: WRITECLIPBOARD blocks
SetClipboardData but does not block EmptyClipboard. The initial ignored
job-ui-access-reference-20261001-r1 probe unexpectedly emptied the host's
clipboard; that side effect was reported to the user and the call was removed
from subsequent native probes. Production leaves EmptyClipboard unchanged.
The durable fixture never empties the clipboard or applies display modes by
default. Its --scratch profile deliberately mutates those resources and must
only run in isolated OsitoK tests, never on the Windows host.

job_ui_access_pe.c runs ten masks in PE32 and PE64, assigns suspended children
before changing the job restrictions, checks live-member visibility and
unaffected parent access, and tests independent read/write/display controls.
It checks all four display wrappers, A/W current-mode queries, error values,
unchanged state after rejected operations, clearing restrictions and invalid
mask atomicity. --partial checks rejection of the still-unimplemented full
mask. --scratch adds real registered-format data, denied non-null writes and
actual unrestricted fullscreen-mode application/restoration. It uses only
test-owned hidden windows, which are destroyed before exit.

### 4.191 Job USER handles and explicit grants

Class 4 now accepts HANDLES (0x01); the implemented mask is 0x37. The remaining
SYSTEMPARAMETERS, DESKTOP and EXITWINDOWS bits (0xc8), including a full 0xff
request, still fail with ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED without changing job state.
This does not yet unblock Chromium's full UI restriction request.

ntjob tracks explicit grants by object kind, handle and owner, independently
for each job. Recognition is allowed for unrestricted callers, same-job
owners, shared system objects or an explicit matching grant. A grant survives
clearing/re-enabling the restriction, but object destruction removes it from
every live job. Final job release frees outstanding grants. The existing
IRQ-saving metadata lock protects membership, grant and lifetime transactions.
UserHandleGrantAccess is exported with three stack arguments for PE32 and
PE64; it validates USER identity and JOB_OBJECT_SET_ATTRIBUTES, treats repeat
grant/revoke requests as successful, and preserves LastError on success.

Stateful USER entry points use public window/menu validation while compositor,
surface, input delivery and teardown retain raw internal lookups. Explicit
insert-after handles, direct built-in control procedures, dialogs, icons,
cursors and input contexts are checked as well. A granted parent can return
an opaque child handle without making that child usable. Internal traversal
of already-validated objects does not incorrectly reclassify their ancestors
or submenus as new API arguments. Shared desktop/cursor handles remain usable;
GetForegroundWindow can still return an opaque inaccessible window handle.

Restricted broadcasts target only top-level windows in the caller's job;
individual window grants do not widen that set. Hook installation checks the
live target thread's process. Cross-process injection of callback modules is
not implemented: local callback addresses fail with error 5 and requests with
a module fail with ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED instead of registering an uncallable
hook. Existing same-process hook dispatch is retained. Hook removal follows
handle grants, and hook/menu numeric namespaces no longer overlap.
PostThreadMessage resolves the real target process but is not denied by the
USER-handle bit; native Windows accepts that operation outside the job too.

Input contexts now retain creating PID/TID and are reclaimed on thread/process
exit, window associations are cleared during teardown, and grants are retired
before handle reuse. A grant makes a foreign HIMC recognizable, not usable as
process-local IMM state. Icon copy/query checks access, including
LR_COPYRETURNORG; a grant does not transfer icon destruction ownership.
These changes do not implement a full IME, global hook injection, new window
stations/desktops, or a security boundary for native CPL0 programs.

Native reference probes use hidden test-owned objects only. The observed
Windows implementation permits an already-authorized job member to grant its
own or another accessible object, despite the blanket member prohibition in
the UserHandleGrantAccess documentation. The fixture records the measured
behavior. A direct foreign standard-control procedure call terminated some
native test children in contract r8; it is not a portable cross-process probe.
The final native profile calls only its own procedure. Rejection of the direct
foreign call is tested only by --scratch inside OsitoK, alongside broadcasts.
No native profile changes clipboard contents, display modes or input focus.

The durable job_ui_handles_pe.c fixture covers grant/revoke/toggle behavior,
independent window/menu/hook/icon/context access, same-job inherited children,
unaffected parent access, error values, rights validation, derived handles,
z-order validation, process-private IMM state and exit cleanup. The QEMU
runner also checks zero live jobs, process records, grants, windows and all
32 input-context slots after each PE32/PE64 run. GitNexus remains unavailable;
manual scope review includes ntjob lifetime/validation, thread identity lookup,

### 4.192 Job system parameters, desktops and session exit

The remaining basic UI bits SYSTEMPARAMETERS (0x08), DESKTOP (0x40) and
EXITWINDOWS (0x80) have enforcement paths. SetInformationJobObject class 4
now accepts the full basic mask 0xff, independently of the existing process
and memory limits. This does not add newer UI flags beyond that basic mask.

SystemParametersInfo A/W distinguish getters, setters and the bidirectional
icon-spacing actions. Restricted writes fail with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED before
touching caller memory or shared state; getters remain available. Unknown
actions reproduce the measured WOW64/native error ordering. Work-area and
wheel-scroll-lines state is shared across A/W; GetMonitorInfo reads the same
work area and listboxes consume the actual wheel setting through an internal
getter, not a guest-pointer API with a kernel-stack output buffer. Work-area
queries continue to follow the live mode by default. Guest buffers are checked
before copying. Unimplemented actions now fail explicitly instead of reporting
success without writing output. Persistence and WM_SETTINGCHANGE broadcast
options remain unsupported and do not mutate state on failure.

CreateDesktopW and SwitchDesktop enforce DESKTOP independently of the other
bits. Switching to the already-active interactive desktop is a no-op; actual
private-desktop compositing remains unsupported and fails explicitly.
ExitWindowsEx enforces EXITWINDOWS but does not pretend to implement a Win32
logoff/shutdown backend for unrestricted callers. Existing private desktop
object metadata and lifetime behavior are retained. All namespace lock users
now save/restore interrupt state, avoiding BSP preemption while holding that
spinlock. The SPI state commit rechecks restrictions with interrupts disabled.

SPI callers, listbox wheel dispatch, GetMonitorInfo, desktop create/switch,
USER-object query/close/process teardown, export ABI metadata and test runners.

### 4.193 Selected-process handle enumeration

NtQueryInformationProcess class 58 now returns a real snapshot of the selected
process's numeric handles, not an empty success or the whole shared table.
GetProcessHandleCount uses the same ownership filtering instead of the global
allocation count. Multiple numeric handles to one object count separately;
shared inherited values occur once per owner. Subsystem-only handles are
excluded except for the three standard console handles already visible through
the existing lookup contract. The global allocation cap is unchanged.

The table is captured under its IRQ-safe lock into a bounded kernel allocation;
no guest output is written while that lock is held. Process resolution and the
snapshot share the existing BSP interrupt exclusion, so termination cannot
recycle the selected process object between them. The snapshot does not retain
objects: a later close can invalidate a returned value, as with Windows.

Native PE32/PE64 reference probes r3/r4 establish the distinct access rules:
enumeration needs QUERY_INFORMATION plus DUP_HANDLE (0x440), while counting
permits QUERY_INFORMATION or QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION. A valid handle to an
exited process reports zero count; table enumeration returns C000010A and zero
ReturnLength. Short buffers fail before handle lookup; successful truncation
reports only whole DWORDs actually copied, regardless of caller pointer width.
Unaligned table output returns DATATYPE_MISALIGNMENT. Invalid guest buffers
return ACCESS_VIOLATION. No broader process-information classes were added.

GitNexus remains unavailable. Manual impact review covers handle ownership and
inheritance, the selected-process resolver, NT query dispatch (including PE32
pseudo-handle conversion), the kernel32 counter and shared fixture runners.

The durable process_handles_pe.c fixture covers real object types, duplicate
versus object counts, truncated prefixes, output sentinels, access masks, child
inheritance, cross-process duplication and close, parent/child isolation, and
exited-process lifetime. A worker performs 256 duplicate/close cycles while the
main thread takes 256 snapshots. Counts return to baseline after the worker.
The scratch profile additionally checks OsitoK's Win32 output-pointer guard;
Windows can raise on that invalid caller pointer rather than return FALSE.
An initial native fixture exposed that difference and was corrected, not used
as an alleged passing oracle.

### 4.195 DisconnectEx completion and TCP ownership (2026-10-02)

The overlap-fixed kernel still reaches a blank Store after ten minutes in
`build/steam-tcp-overlap-20261002-r1/`. At tick 63895, 29 CLOSED, claimed TCP
records have neither a live WinSock handle nor a duplication token. The
subsequent `steam-tcp-retire-20261002-r1/fault-trace.log` records Steam calling
`net_tcp_shutdown` from `wsock_disconnect_ex` without `net_tcp_release`;
ordinary closesocket calls in the same trace do release their records.
This establishes a transport-ownership leak on an API Steam actually uses,
not proof that every unowned record or the physical spinner has that cause.

The old DisconnectEx also ignored OVERLAPPED and returned success without
posting completion. Its replacement validates flags, the reserved argument,
socket state and the PE32/PE64 OVERLAPPED range. A pending request owns the
detached TCP record through graceful close, then releases it exactly once.
The global network worker completes requests in their owner's address space;
event and IOCP notification use the existing completion helpers. Synchronous
callers wait without holding the socket lifecycle lock. Cancellation, socket
close and process teardown retire pending requests rather than abandoning
their records. Pending reads are canceled before the shared handle can refer
to a new connection. Duplicated handles and unconsumed duplication tokens
receive the disconnected/reusable state. ConnectEx reuse requires
TF_REUSE_SOCKET; the IOCP association and local binding are preserved.

This does not grow the TCP table, reclaim arbitrary CLOSED records, disable
the browser sandbox, or change Steam arguments. The existing TCP close
timeout/TIME_WAIT policy remains unchanged. Other teardown paths, including
WSACleanup and process exit for sockets without a pending DisconnectEx,
still need their own ownership audit.

`build-disconnect-test.sh` builds the freestanding public-API fixture for
both ABIs. Windows x86/x64 pass the completion/reuse/duplicate/invalid-argument
and pending-read checks (57), 96 synchronous disconnect cycles (586 checks),
and 96 CancelIoEx/closesocket cycles (1210 checks). The same three modes also
pass when launched in a child process; native results are retained in
`disconnect-native-20261002-r3/` and `disconnect-native-20261002-r5/`.
The lifetime mode starts 32 children, each exiting with three pending
disconnects, for 96 abandoned requests per ABI. Both Windows
`disconnect-native-20261002-r7/` and the final-kernel QEMU run
`disconnect-lifetime-positive-20261002-r1/` pass all 266 parent checks;
every child reports three genuinely pending requests. This tests pending
DisconnectEx teardown, not arbitrary process-exit socket cleanup.

### 4.196 Ordinary process-exit TCP claims (2026-10-02)

The next ownership audit finds a separate leak in
`wsock_release_backend_on_process_exit`: it aborts the last reference's TCP
connection but does not release its claim. `net_tcp_abort` closes transport
state and wakes waiters; allocation still requires an unclaimed CLOSED slot.
The helper now releases the claim immediately after abort. Its existing
lifecycle lock and final-reference check cover both socket handles and
unconsumed WSADuplicateSocket tokens addressed to the exiting process.
Live references in another process must remain usable, consistent with the
[shared socket contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-wsaduplicatesocketw).
There is no TCP-table growth, global CLOSED-record sweep, or change to normal
closesocket, WSACleanup, ConnectEx/AcceptEx cancellation or linger semantics.
Those other teardown paths still need their own audit.

The public-API fixture adds two modes:

- `--orphans` runs 32 children that each leave three TCP connections open.
  Windows x86/x64 pass 266 parent checks in `socket-exit-native-20261002-r1/`.
  On the frozen 4.195 kernel, `socket-exit-negative-20261002-r1/` fails at
  child 21: `exit-open connect` check 14 and parent check 172, with an explicit
  `No free connection slots` diagnostic. The new image passes both ABIs in
  `socket-exit-positive-20261002-r1/`, including SSH after the fixtures.
- `--tokens` creates 128 suspended children with an unconsumed duplication
  token, then lets each exit. Alternating rounds close the source first or
  retain it and verify data transfer after the target exits. Both Windows
  ABIs pass 1354 checks in `socket-exit-native-20261002-r2/`. QEMU PE32 passes
  in `socket-token-positive-20261002-r1/`; PE64 passes the same 1354 checks in
  the isolated `socket-token-positive64-20261002-r1/` run.

The token negative control on the frozen 4.195 kernel,
`socket-token-negative-20261002-r1/`, fails `connect` at check 1322 after
reporting 96 completed rounds. The positive token runs retain working SSH.
The new image also passes both ABI deadline fixtures and the general IOCP
and WinSock shell selftests in `socket-exit-iocp-regression-20261002-r1/`.
Python compilation, shell-script syntax and scoped diff whitespace checks
pass. This does not claim another full Steam load test on the local image.

The combined token run is not an all-pass: after PE32 finishes, PE64 reaches
`No free process slot` at child PID 253 and fails its launch check 1303.
The headless boot path intentionally does not start the zombie reaper, so
this two-ABI sequence accumulates exited child slots. The PE64-only rerun
isolates the socket contract; it does not resolve headless process reaping
or erase the failed combined run. No process-table/reaper change is included.

Ethernet TX/RX drop counters are 1049/1330. These are observed drops, not an
established explanation for Steam's application-level encryption error.
The user confirms that sign-in is still in progress. No stop, hotreload or
reboot was sent during this observation, and the library remains unverified.

### 4.197 Physical Steam performance: USB startup and post-login waits (2026-10-02)

Performance observations separate startup from the later user-data spinner.
The initial read-only P1 captures in `p1-performance-20261002-r1/` show
46.77-48.04% BSP C0 residency, about 2.69 GHz while active, 54 C without
thermal/critical/PROCHOT flags, and 44,654 MiB free of 48,599 MiB. These
samples do not support RAM exhaustion or thermal throttling as the dominant
cause. They are one logical CPU's samples, not whole-machine utilization.
Sequential short SSH commands return in roughly 0.3-0.5 seconds, although
shell tail of a large log can take much longer: its implementation scans
the entire file in 8 KiB chunks. Verified 32 KiB random-range file reads in
`p1-performance-20261002-r3/` take 0.062-0.103 seconds. Their hash-only
requests still involve disk and protocol work, so they are not a pure disk
bandwidth benchmark. Earlier r1/r2 helper failures were an oversized sync
request and a missing close between opens, not kernel transport failures.

The old profiler could not answer this question: its address-indexed bins
excluded the upper-half kernel and normal PE images, its report consumed
the histogram, and the timer vector also counted software sched_yield calls.
`kprof` now starts explicitly and resets a bounded 1024-entry hashed
histogram plus a 4096-entry chronological ring. Samples retain full RIP,
actual CR3, PID and tick; user address spaces remain distinct. LAPIC ISR
bit 32 filters software INT 0x20 before EOI, and at most one sample is kept
per virtual 100 Hz tick. The interrupt path has bounded probes and no
allocation or output. Reports copy under a brief BSP IRQ mask, then format
outside it, without consuming results. Overflow and skipped events are
reported. This is BSP timer sampling, not NMI sampling or all-CPU wall time.
The LAPIC ISR distinction follows the Local APIC interrupt acceptance rules
in the [Intel SDM, Volume 3A](https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/835754/253668-sdm-vol-3a.pdf);
it does not make IRQ-masked execution observable.

Authenticated diagnostics now admit only `kprof`, `kprof start`,
`kprof stop`, `kprof raw`, `sched stats`, `perf`, `perf snapshot` and
`serial-stats` while a foreground application owns the console. Unknown
arguments, bare `sched` (which launches workers), and `perf reset` are not
added to the independent diagnostic set. GitNexus is unavailable; manual
impact review covers the BSP sampling hook, shell admission/dispatch and
host/QEMU fixtures. No timer frequency or scheduler policy is changed.

Validation artifacts under `arch/x86/build/`:

- `kprof-host-20261002-r1/`: GCC/Clang normal and ASan/UBSan, each passing
  74,238 checks for address/CR3 separation, software/tick filters, IRQ-safe
  snapshots, non-destructive reports, allocation failure and bounded overflow.
- `kprof-shell-host-20261002-r1/`: all four configurations pass 172 admission
  checks. `kprof-qemu-20261002-r1/` passes all 16 SSH/maintenance gates,
  including real PE32/PE64 samples, frozen repeated reports, capture,
  output isolation and cooperative stop while local workers are runnable.
- `kprof-ssh-regression-20261002-r1/`: all 28 gates pass, including binary
  delta sync, interrupted transfer, cold-boot persistence and kexec reconnect.
  The normal clang kernel build and scoped whitespace checks also pass.

After preserving physical request 6's logs/capture and announcing the
interruption, cooperative stop returns the console to idle. Verified sync

The frozen image in `kprof-qemu-20261002-r1/kernel.elf` is 7,342,648 bytes,
SHA-256 `39b4f6fb2b64fd423f621b7746f5d53259dc79591ce7589ca1fe489b1b88aaea`.
It includes the section 4.196 ordinary process-exit fix, now deployed.

this image is not tested here.

Four sequential, approximately 20-second P1 profiles use that exact ELF:

| Artifact prefix (each ends in `-20261002-r1/`) | Sampled evidence | BSP C0 snapshot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `p1-kprof-idle` | 1922/1935 samples at `cpu_idle_wait`, 13 in GUI alpha fill | 4.24% |
| `p1-kprof-steam-start` | 1917/1933 samples in `usb_storage_read` | 99.48% |
| `p1-kprof-steam-later` | 1874/1929 samples in `usb_storage_read` | 99.48% |
| `p1-kprof-steam-loaded` | 1420/1520 samples at idle, 57 GUI alpha fill, 19 FS writes | 44.21% before, 24.75% after |

All four retain zero histogram drops and zero raw-ring overwrites. The
startup concentration is specifically `0xFFFF800002170B0F`, just after
STI in the inlined `usb_io_unlock_irqrestore`. It is not evidence that this
instruction itself consumes 97-99% of wall time: pending timer interrupts
are delivered there after masked intervals. Code inspection confirms the
whole synchronous BOT transaction holds the IRQ-save lock, while xHCI
polls for completion. The near-100% C0 measurements independently show a
busy CPU during that loading phase. Disabling interrupts across USB I/O
also delays scheduling and network servicing. A timer profile alone cannot
measure the interior or duration of each such masked interval.

There is an additional concrete batching limit: `disk_read_bytes` only
passes aligned NVMe reads directly to the driver. USB uses an 8 KiB
physically backed bounce buffer, so one 64 KiB filesystem read becomes
eight BOT commands, each with CBW/data/CSW phases. The USB driver itself can
read up to 128 sectors (64 KiB for this device) per command. Larger safe
batches and an interruptible wait with preserved BOT ownership are the
next storage targets; simply removing the lock or passing arbitrary user
buffers to DMA is not a valid fix. Larger batches alone could lengthen a
single masked interval and must be measured. Existing immutable DLL source
caching is already present; cache-hit effectiveness was not measured here.
The boot's `Full (12Mbps)` port line precedes reset and is not proof of the
actual negotiated transfer speed after enumeration.

After loading, the verified 1920x1080 capture still shows `Loading user
data...`, not a library. The current-run connection log in
`p1-kprof-steam-current-20261002-r1/` records login OK at 01:53:18 followed
by `Encryption Failure` at 01:53:20, another OK at 01:53:25, then the same
failure at 01:55:49 and further reconnection. These are current entries,
not only historical logs. The lower later C0 readings and repeated
connection failures distinguish this phase from CPU-saturated loading.
The encryption-error root cause remains open; faster storage alone cannot
be claimed to fix it.

The later WLAN snapshot reports a legacy 54,000 kbps TX rate, channel 6,
open data port, firmware completion 2664/2664 with zero failures, and
software TX/RX drops 94/10. The driver currently uses legacy 20 MHz SISO,
16-frame software queues and a single pending data DMA transmission; AP
capacity of 600 Mbps is not the implemented client throughput. These
cumulative drops do not establish the encryption error's cause. The
compressed remote capture transfers 491,088 wire bytes in 40.992 seconds,
despite short SSH queries continuing to succeed, so sustained transfer
latency also remains a separate measurement target. No USB, filesystem
batching or WLAN throughput optimization is claimed by this instrumentation
change. Steam is left open and profiling stopped after collecting evidence.

### 4.198 USB read batching and physical retest (2026-10-02)

The first storage optimization from 4.197 is implemented and deployed:
`disk_read_bytes` sizes physically backed USB bounce buffers up to 64 KiB,
with an 8 KiB allocation fallback. It does not remove BOT serialization,
enable scheduling inside a live DMA request or change file-write semantics.
The new PE32/PE64 fixture checks every byte, EOF and partial boundaries, and
times 8/64 KiB reads through the public Win32 API. Both ABIs pass native
Windows, QEMU xHCI USB storage and the physical P1. The byte-layer negative
control, sanitized host tests, full USB SSH regression and deployment hash
are recorded in [the USB read-batch report](x86-usb-storage.md#bounded-usb-read-batches-2026-10-02).

Physical PE64 64 KiB requests read 2 MiB in 89-97 ms versus 173-175 ms before;
the smaller-request control also changes across hotreload, so this is not
a claim that all of Steam is twice as fast. Startup still samples at the
USB IRQ-restore boundary. After updating both persistent kernel copies and
hotreloading, Steam is launched naturally as console request 4. The captured
screen shows the full login form and QR, with SSH functioning. It is left
open for local sign-in. A successful physical library transition and the
post-login Encryption Failure are still unverified on this image.

### 4.199 Direct USB timing identifies small-read startup pressure

The timer profiler's USB restore samples are now supplemented by elapsed TSC
accounting, available as read-only `usb-perf` during foreground Win32 execution.

locations, followed by automatic hotreload reconnection.

During the natural Steam startup, one 20.292-second interval makes 49,928
reads averaging 2048 bytes. USB read ownership masks interrupts for 18.599
seconds (91.66%); ownership acquisition costs only 1.238 ms. No USB failure
occurs. The bootstrap log places executable checksum verification in a
105-second interval overlapping this burst. The exact native reader is not
yet traced. Small file reads are not coalesced by the larger byte-layer
bounce buffer, and OsitoFS3 currently caches metadata, not file contents.

After startup, a separate 20.426-second interval spends only 0.100% holding

See [direct USB wait accounting](x86-usb-storage.md#direct-usb-wait-accounting-2026-10-02)
for contracts, measurements, deployment hash and all host/QEMU evidence.
Coherent small-read caching and interruptible DMA ownership are separate
pending changes; no app-specific verification bypass is introduced.

### 4.200 Bounded buffered reads coalesce small requests

`NtReadFile` now uses revision-checked read windows, with at most 2 MiB of
fixed cache data. Read-ahead adapts to consecutive offsets, honors explicit
sequential/random/no-buffering options, falls back on allocation or speculative
read failure, and preserves the existing byte-range checks, offsets and EOF.
`CreateFileA/W` now forward these options instead of dropping them. Last-close
cookies prevent cache reuse across recycled file objects; no loading slot or
cache lock is held across disk I/O. Filesystem writers and USB ownership are
unchanged; arbitrary mid-I/O thread cancellation is not newly qualified.

The same verified 2 MiB / 2 KiB-read fixture requires 1068 USB reads on the
previous kernel and 77 on the new kernel, for both PE32 and PE64, including
executable loading overhead. Random and unbuffered controls remain at 1068
(1069 for PE64 random). Peer writes, truncation/growth, lock conflicts, EOF,
duplicate handles and exit without explicit close all pass, as do the native
Windows executions. This isolates the small-read optimization but does not
measure a physical Steam launch or solve the later encryption/network failure.

See [buffered NT read windows](x86-usb-storage.md#buffered-nt-read-windows-2026-10-02)
for memory/lifetime boundaries, host concurrency/sanitizer tests, old-kernel
negative control and artifact hash. The P1 remains unreachable over SSH and
has not received this image. The user reports the link-triggered breakpoint at
`0x1859EF906` after clicking a help link below the login QR. This matches the
saved libcef image's fatal delay-load-failure path (also seen for a different
missing import in 4.168). The specific DLL/export for this click is not yet
captured; neither the address alone nor the cache tests establish that cause.

### 4.201 Reject corrupt TCP segments before delivering stream bytes

The shared TCP stack lacked receive checksum validation, even though its NIC
contract does not guarantee hardware validation. The new guard rejects invalid
pseudo-header/header/data checksums before touching state or acknowledging bytes,
including control-only segments and loopback. It does not change WinSock APIs,
connection ownership, encryption or advertised offload features.

An old-source negative control accepts and acknowledges a single-bit payload
corruption; the corrected source rejects it and accepts the valid retransmission.
All nine RX groups, TX/MSS/passive/link/waiter regressions pass in all four host
compiler/sanitizer configurations. The combined cache/checksum kernel also passes
28 USB SSH gates and the eight private-process PE32/PE64 external-network gates.
Both ABIs pass the separate eight-gate loopback/DisconnectEx profile as well.
See [TCP receive checksum validation](x86-network-stack.md#19-validate-tcp-receive-checksums-2026-10-02)
for exact boundaries, artifacts and the frozen image hash. It is not yet deployed
to the P1, and no physical Steam encryption failure or link breakpoint is declared
resolved by these controlled tests.

The same combined image is now installed in both physical P1 kernel locations.
After kexec, saved 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, DHCP and SSH return automatically. Steam's
unchanged executable checksum verification takes 25 seconds instead of 105 in
the prior physical run, and the verified screenshot shows the complete login
and QR. This proves improvement of that storage-heavy phase, not total Steam
readiness. The new launch and post-login dmesg contain no TCP bad-checksum
drops. After sign-in the screenshot shows `Loading user data...`; the current
connection log again records logon OK followed by `Encryption Failure` about
two minutes later. The link breakpoint still lacks a causal missing-import
trace. See the physical buffered-read
section in `x86-usb-storage.md` for intervals, artifacts and remaining IRQ-off
latency. No physical cold-boot qualification is claimed from hotreload.

### 4.203 Large Winsock streams: public-API integrity qualification

The recurring post-login Encryption Failure is still unexplained. A new
`winsock_stream_pe.c` fixture tests an independent byte-stream contract before
changing the transport or cryptography. PE32 and PE64 each create a private
child process, receive 2 MiB of offset-dependent data and transmit a different
2 MiB pattern. Every byte is checked, including partial reads/writes and EOF;
the host independently verifies the outgoing stream and records both hashes.
This is synthetic data, not Steam traffic or captured credentials.

Mode 0 uses blocking `recv` with intermittent `MSG_PEEK`. Mode 1 posts up to
three overlapped `WSARecv` operations, each with scatter buffers including a
zero-length entry, checks guards and completion identity/count/status, and
transmits through overlapped `WSASend`. Completed receives are verified in
submission order, not completion order, following Microsoft's
[overlapped I/O contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/overlapped-i-o-and-event-objects-2).
Stack WSABUF descriptors are cleared with volatile writes after submission to exercise the
[provider's descriptor-capture obligation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-wsarecv).
Object-code inspection found that the initial ordinary memset was optimized
away. The final r3 fixture retains the stores on both ABIs; all results below
refer to the r2 test runs repeated with that corrected fixture.
Socket operations, completion waits and child lifetime have finite timeouts.
No shim, TCP or driver implementation changes accompany this fixture.

`build-winsock-stream-test.sh` builds both ABIs with warnings as errors.
`test-winsock-stream-native.py` passes all four ABI/mode combinations on
Windows (`winsock-stream-native-20261002-r2/`). The opt-in
`OSITO_SSH_TEST_WINSOCK_STREAM=1` QEMU profile passes eleven gates, including
the four private-process cases and independent host TX verification
(`winsock-stream-qemu-20261002-r2/`). The profile uses disposable NVMe storage
and virtio networking, not the P1's USB/AX200 devices. Both runs transfer
16 MiB in total, with matching per-direction SHA-256 values:

- RX: `b1d31640a97e912c035396a92a84190b1a23016799345af1785f99b908a551e9`
- TX: `a2db40532a256528070107dc9e7248b3507675d32a44f186f5e037c5da14866d`

Native `--corrupt-at 131075` and QEMU
`OSITO_SSH_TEST_STREAM_CORRUPT=131075` flip exactly one received byte. All four
combinations reject it at that exact offset, exit unsuccessfully and terminate
their transfer; the server observes reset rather than a false success. The
negative artifacts are `winsock-stream-native-negative-20261002-r2/` and
`winsock-stream-qemu-negative-20261002-r2/`. SSH remains responsive after each
QEMU case. This is a test-oracle negative control, not an older-kernel failure.
The QEMU image is the unchanged 4.202 frozen kernel, SHA-256
`856db8fc1246f7af26758cfcd92857d701444569a4d8ab638d70998360a2abeb`.

### 4.204 Identify the actual Steam TLS implementation before changing it

The P1 import-table audit and a complete revision-checked download identify
the current `steamclient64.dll` as PE64, 26,328,216 bytes, SHA-256
`caba4826aa3501039d095aee1843a6bfb270fb43a3ab4455b2d6733223579fee`.
The QEMU base contains the identical DLL. The old PE32 static reference is
not used to infer this client's x64 transport. This DLL embeds OpenSSL 1.1.1i;
its CRYPT32 imports cover certificate operations and bcrypt supplies random
bytes. The generic result string Encryption Failure (EResult 23) does not
identify the failing cryptographic operation.

The ignored `steam-tls-trace-20261002.py` diagnostic uses bounded hardware
breakpoints at the embedded TLS handshake and error formatter. Before reading
metadata it compares runtime PE identity and instruction bytes with the exact
reference DLL. It records error codes, constant error descriptions and code
addresses, not application payloads, keys or raw stack contents. No inferior
function calls or binary patches are used. These offsets are version-specific
diagnostics, not production compatibility behavior.

`steam-tls-fresh-20261002-r1/` runs the frozen 4.202 kernel for 300 seconds
with a fresh scratch profile and no account login. Four verified handshake
entries fire the bounded handshake probe; the error probe never fires. Steam
renders its login form and QR. All fifteen SSH maintenance probes pass at
60/180/300 seconds, remote capture works, an exclusive command is refused
while the console is busy, and cooperative stop completes. This does not
qualify post-login TLS or reproduce the physical Encryption Failure.

The serial trace is not otherwise clean: it contains one new `win32_process`
with RIP zero and no prior saved CS/RIP. Investigation led to 4.205. The P1
remained on request 3 with working pinned SSH and pre-login CM retries during
this run; no new successful login or library readiness was observed.

### 4.205 Populate every Win32 child entry point

`MAX_WIN32_CHILDREN` was 32 but `win32_child_entries` only initialized sixteen
entries. C silently zero-filled slots 16..31. On the seventeenth concurrent
child, `win32_spawn_child` handed NULL to the scheduler, which rejected RIP
zero; the creator remained waiting for a creation acknowledgement that could
never arrive. This is a deterministic creation deadlock, not evidence that
the child itself corrupted its saved frame. Steam's QEMU trace encountered
the same zero-entry signature while launching a service child.

One slot list now generates both all 32 entry wrappers and their pointer
table. The table has inferred length, with a compile-time assertion against
the context capacity, so enlarging only the capacity cannot silently create
NULL entries again. No scheduler, TLS, networking or capacity policy changes
are part of this fix. GitNexus is unavailable; manual impact is the child
entry dispatch table and its single consumer, `win32_spawn_child`.

`child_capacity_pe.c` creates 31 suspended children before resuming any,
checks distinct identities and their STILL_ACTIVE status, resumes every
entry, verifies exit code 83, closes handles and repeats the full wave. An
Osito-only `--limit` check also requires the next creation to fail normally:
the separate NT object table has 32 entries including the parent. This test
does not claim 32 simultaneous children or a dynamic process limit.

- Native Windows PE32 and PE64 each pass both waves with the final fixture.
- The frozen old kernel reproduces a zero-RIP scheduler rejection at child
  17 on both ABIs (`child-capacity-negative{32,64}-20261002-r2/`). These runs
  intentionally dispose the VM with the creator still waiting; they do not
  attempt normal teardown of the broken state.
- `child-capacity-qemu-20261002-r2/` passes all nine gates: both ABI capacity,
  exhaustion and reuse cases, plus SSH checks before and after the workload.
  The first positive run exposed the legitimate NT parent-inclusive limit;
  the final fixture uses 31 children rather than raising that limit.
- `make -C arch/x86 CLANG=1 QUIET=1 SKIP_MODEL=1 -j6` succeeds. The frozen
  candidate is 7,352,288 bytes, SHA-256
  `86b294d93ae697a0afcda10cf0f3391a460ae5c44b9ed31b70882f14ebb5a823`.
  The existing unused `process_peb` warning remains.

The subsequent `steam-child-capacity-20261002-r1/` scratch run reaches the login
form without scheduler corruption. All fifteen periodic SSH checks pass and
cooperative stop completes. It is not an all-green maintenance run: remote
